title: Cancellation and timeouts
sub: CancellationToken: a polite request to stop
cards/0/body: Cancellation in .NET is cooperative: a CancellationTokenSource hands out a token, you pass it to methods, and they check it and stop on their own. You can't forcibly "kill" a task.
cards/1/q: The server didn't answer within 5 seconds. What happens?
cards/1/options/0: The token is canceled, and GetStringAsync throws OperationCanceledException
cards/1/explain: HttpClient throws TaskCanceledException, which derives from OperationCanceledException.
cards/2/title: Your own code must listen too
cards/2/body: In a long loop, call token.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() and pass the token on to every async method. Otherwise cancellation gets stuck at your method.
cards/3/explain: SaveAsync never got the token, so a save in progress won't be interrupted.
cards/4/q: How do you cancel a task that doesn't accept a token?
cards/4/options/0: Not directly: you can only stop waiting for it, e.g. with WaitAsync(token)
cards/4/explain: WaitAsync (.NET 6+) stops the waiting, but the operation itself keeps running in the background.
cards/5/q: Which are true? Select all that apply.
cards/5/options/2: You can create a CancellationTokenSource with a timeout
cards/5/options/4: Checking the token at the end of the method is enough
cards/5/explain: Code stops only where it checks the token.
cards/6/explain: You pass the token itself to methods, not the source.
